title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
An AI system was used to create a fake interview featuring real public figures, Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock and ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler, discussing an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The deepfake article was deployed in a scam to deceive consumers into investing. This failure occurred at the point where the system was used for impersonation and fraud rather than legitimate purposes.

The scam combined AI-generated deepfake content with fabricated websites, articles, and advertisements to build false credibility. No human verification appears to have stopped the content before it reached potential victims. What would have caught this is platform moderation that checks whether interview subjects actually consented to and participated in published content.

It is not established how the AI system was initially built or what guardrails it contained. The scam reflects a deployment choice by fraudsters to use AI for impersonation, not a failure of the system's design to prevent such use.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
# Summary

A fake online article featured Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock in a fabricated heated interview with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler about Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The interview never actually occurred. This type of scam, using artificial intelligence to create convincing deepfake content featuring celebrities and politicians, is rapidly increasing in Australia. ASIC's new research shows that investment scams utilizing AI-generated images and videos of well-known figures are becoming more sophisticated and harder to detect.

ASIC removed 19,400 scams last year, a 182 percent increase, including 7,051 fake investment platforms and 5,476 phishing scams. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese tops the list of impersonated public figures, along with politicians like Pauline Hanson and business leaders including Alan Kohler and Dick Smith. Scammers build elaborate fake online footprints combining fake websites, articles, and advertisements to deceive consumers. ASIC advises people to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers and independently check company details before investing. Kohler argues that platforms hosting such content should face heavy fines.
